summary: Del Mar packs fewer than 4,000 residents into just 1.8 square miles of coastal bluff terrain wedged between the Pacific Ocean and the Los Peñasquitos Lagoon — a footprint so small that the entire city is roughly the size of a single large golf course community, yet it hosts one of the most famous thoroughbred horse-racing venues in North America at the Del Mar Racetrack. The median home value exceeds $2 million against a median household income near $193,000, yielding a price-to-income ratio above 10:1 — meaning even at the local median income, purchasing requires substantial existing wealth or assets beyond salary. With 8.8 hours of daily sunshine on average and annual daytime highs hovering around 70°F, the climate is remarkably temperate year-round, rarely swinging into genuine heat or cold. The city itself is not a job center; it functions largely as a residential enclave along the I-5 corridor, with most employment concentrated in biotech, defense, and healthcare clusters in neighboring Sorrento Valley, Torrey Pines, and greater San Diego. Camino Del Mar, the main north-south street, carries a small but distinct strip of restaurants, boutiques, and coffee shops above the beach, giving the commercial core a compact, walkable feel — though beyond that strip, the hilly residential streets are quiet and car-dependent. Property crime runs notably high at 1,849 per 100,000, driven largely by larceny, a pattern consistent with high-traffic tourist and racetrack areas adjacent to residential zones. Del Mar is essentially a two-mile stretch of ocean-bluff real estate where the entry price buys proximity to one of Southern California's best microclimates, but almost nothing about daily employment or errands stays within city limits.
